title: The Investor Who Told William Tanuwijaya He Was Not Special
dek: From 2007 to 2009 a young Jakarta web worker pitched an online marketplace to anyone with money; his own boss finally backed it, and Tokopedia opened in August 2009.

story.founder: William Tanuwijaya and Leontinus Alpha Edison
story.event: Pitching for two years before the first money for an online marketplace in Jakarta
story.summary: From 2007 William Tanuwijaya, a Jakarta web worker from North Sumatra, pitched an online marketplace to potential investors, who doubted that an Indonesian without a famous name or university could build one; Bloomberg reported that it took eleven pitches. In February 2009 his employer's owner, Victor Fungkong, backed the company himself, and Tanuwijaya and Leontinus Alpha Edison launched Tokopedia on 17 August 2009. Venture investors followed from 2010, including SoftBank and Sequoia in 2014.
paragraphs: In 2008 a would-be investor gave William Tanuwijaya some advice. "William, don't waste your time," he recalled being told: the people who started Amazon, Facebook and Google were special, and he was not. Tanuwijaya, then in his mid-twenties and working in Jakarta, had been pitching since 2007 for an online marketplace where Indonesians who had never met could trust each other enough to trade. Bloomberg later reported that it took eleven pitches to get funding.

He had nothing to fall back on. He had come to Jakarta from Pematangsiantar in North Sumatra and paid for university with three years of twelve-hour night shifts at an internet café. His father had cancer, and as the family's only earner he kept his job while he pitched. Investors asked him to name one Indonesian who had built a successful internet business, warned that eBay, Rakuten or Alibaba would take the market, and asked about his family, his university and his lack of experience. "The people who rejected me only asked me about my past, which I couldn't change," he said later.

He kept going. "I decided right then that I will never give up on myself," he told Bloomberg in 2016. The only person he knew with money, he said, was the owner of the group he worked for, Victor Fungkong, who had heard the first pitch and introduced him to others. When none of them invested, Fungkong backed the company himself. On 6 February 2009 he signed the deed setting up PT Tokopedia; by one account he put in Rp 2.4 billion for 80 per cent, with Tanuwijaya and his colleague Leontinus Alpha Edison holding 10 per cent each.

A team of four spent about six months building the site, testing it with some 70 merchants. Tokopedia opened on 17 August 2009, and the first order arrived within twelve minutes, he said. Outside money followed: East Ventures in 2010, then other Japanese and Korean investors, who, he said, put up with his limited English, and in October 2014 $100 million from SoftBank and Sequoia Capital. He raised money every year from 2009 to 2014 and said each investor taught him something new.

quote.text: I shall never be a Milo, and yet I do not neglect my body; nor shall I be a Croesus, and yet I do not neglect my property; nor, in a word, do we neglect looking after anything because we despair of reaching the highest degree.
quote.locator: Book I, chapter 2, "How a man on every occasion can maintain his proper character"
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: The investor said Tanuwijaya was not one of the special few. Epictetus, a former slave, does not argue the point. He says that never becoming the strongest wrestler or the richest king is no reason to stop tending what is in your care, which is a steadier ground than believing you are exceptional.

reflection: The investor's verdict was about where Tanuwijaya came from: no famous university, no family money, no Indonesian example to point to. He could not change any of that. What he could change was how often he asked, and how good the next pitch was.

Epictetus offers something quieter than "believe in yourself". You do not have to think you are exceptional to keep looking after the work in front of you. Some mornings you will feel entirely ordinary, and that is allowed. An ordinary day of careful work still counts.
invitation: If someone's doubt about your background is still sitting with you, write down the one question about your work you would rather they had asked. Then answer it for yourself in three sentences.

cross_checks.claim: Tanuwijaya pitched from 2007 and was turned down by investors who doubted an Indonesian without a famous name could build a marketplace.
The first money came in February 2009 from his employer's owner, Victor Fungkong, through PT Indonusa Dwitama.
He worked night shifts at an internet cafe while studying, and his father was ill.
East Ventures invested in 2010, and SoftBank and Sequoia put in $100 million in October 2014.

research_notes: The investor's words differ by telling: in 2016 (Bloomberg, via Malay Mail) Tanuwijaya quoted a 2008 investor saying 'William, don't waste your time' and that the founders of Amazon, Facebook and Google were special; in 2017 (Selular.ID, in Indonesian) the advice is rendered 'youth comes only once, so find a more realistic dream'; in 2021 (CNBC) it is 'Please stop daydreaming; find something more realistic to do.' The story quotes the 2016 version, dated 2008, and attributes it. The number of pitches (eleven) comes only from Bloomberg's 2016 report and is attributed to it. First money: AVCJ and Selular say his boss or former boss backed it in February 2009 (Selular gives 6 February); Good News From Indonesia names Victor Fungkong, gives the deed date of 6 February 2009 and Rp 2.4 billion for 80 per cent; Tempo (2019, which returns 403 and is not cited) is reported to give Rp 2.5 billion; CNBC calls PT Indonusa Dwitama the seed investor; a 2024 Kompasiana blog (not cited) dates Indonusa's first investment to 2010. The story uses February 2009 and gives the Rp 2.4 billion figure as 'one account'. Good News From Indonesia calls Fungkong a de facto co-founder; the story names him as the backer. Leontinus Alpha Edison is credited as co-founder by CNBC and as Tanuwijaya's colleague at Fungkong's group from 2007 by Good News From Indonesia; little in the loadable sources describes his own part in the fundraising, so the story keeps his role brief. Age: born 11 November 1981 (BINUS), so 26 or 27 in 2008. Bloomberg's original article and Tokopedia's own Medium history return 403; the Bloomberg text is cited from Malay Mail's republication, which credits Bloomberg. Epictetus's remark is applied by analogy.
